title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
description: A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and ou
body: A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served.The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured to replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue.His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints. It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy, but it did not comment on the rats claim.Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location.Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues.The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House.Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September.Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter.Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead.A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation."Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice.The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern".He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant."I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said.Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date.Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings.A spokesperson for Soho House apologised for the incident, saying: "This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy."They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted."Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added."For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling."Soho House membership starts from £291.67 monthly or £204.17 for under-27s.The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses.The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity.It was bought by a consortium of investors last year, with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board.

schema.headline: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety

title: Chris Mason: Andy Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
description: What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a gener
body: What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like – the idea being that the argument is won in advance. Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest. But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock – note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals – it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and – after a review to come – the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union. How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.And from the longer term stuff to the here and now – including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Andy Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core

title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
description: On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told
body: On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK  Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.For a while it was unclear whether the men were already being watched by undercover surveillance teams when they were spotted by villagers in the dead of night, or whether the villagers really were the first people to alert the police.Taylor has now given some assistance on this, saying the response on Sunday morning was "due to a range of information that we received", suggesting the police had some other intelligenceCertainly security had been visibly stepped up at the base in the preceding days, so certainly there had been some intelligence about a possible attack. Elite firearms officers were very quick to respond to the villagers' 999 calls.Both counter-terrorism and military sources have told me that this story is still quite near the beginning, raising the possibility that detectives are trying to identify some kind of "controlling hand" behind the presence of the suspects in Whelford with their petrol.That leaves a number of options open:The men could be entirely innocent and able to give a good explanation for being in Whelford on SundayThey could have been paid or tricked into moving the vehicles and the petrol, but unaware of who they were working forOr they could have been part of a plot which was interrupted before it reached a more dangerous phaseThat is why the next bit of the counter-terrorism investigation is so vital. By examining mobile phones and computers, tracking vehicles, searching addresses, and using the covert techniques of MI5, GCHQ and US intelligence, detectives are trying to build a clearer picture.On that critical investigation rests the decision over whether to arrest anyone else, whether to charge the five men, and whether we ever find out the true story of the mysterious RAF Fairford plot.

schema.headline: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?

title: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
description: The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues duri
body: The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group.Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, will leave his job at the end of the year, the company SETE said in a statement.It said an internal investigation found that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of female staff.They were replaced by male colleagues as a delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the Eiffel Tower earlier this month.BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.At the time, SETE said the Hindu delegation had requested that the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted".A staff union representative said "women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated". Staff at the monument said female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".The visit led to the closure of the tower as staff went on strike to show their outrage and politicians condemned the incident.Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said after the visit: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, called it an "absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision" and ordered two separate investigations.SETE chair Ariel Weil said on Tuesday that he had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented. "The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions," he said.

schema.headline: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit

title: 'Mum sent them £140,000': How to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed
description: In a bid to get her mum to open up, Helen decided "to try and be calm about this and open up the possibility she could trust me". Dale Richardson, a p
body: In a bid to get her mum to open up, Helen decided "to try and be calm about this and open up the possibility she could trust me". Dale Richardson, a police fraud protect officer, encourages families to be "curious but not confrontational". "I like to break it down... and listen to them and say, right, how did you meet? And what have they said?"Helen convinced her mum to allow her to speak to the scammer on a video call.She says she quickly spotted the deepfake as the image was "fuzzy" and his voice out of sync with his movements.Helen tried to convince her mum the man she was speaking to was not who he said he was but she did not believe her."She was saying I made her feel disgusted and ashamed," says Helen. "And that I should let her have her relationship and not intervene."Forensic linguist Dr Lis Carter, who is part of the Scam Secrets team, stresses the importance of being patient and careful with your words when trying to help loved ones who believe they are in a genuine relationship."Being a family member coming into that, you are 'destroying' that happiness." Unable to break her mum away from the scam, Helen turned to her bank. She had a lasting power of attorney, meaning she could act on behalf of her mum and set up safeguards for her accounts.Jim Winters, head of economic crime at Nationwide, says anyone who believes a family member is being scammed should contact their bank."They might be limited in what they can share with you for data privacy reasons, but they can take steps to safeguard that account," he says."Once we know that a customer is being defrauded we can spot the hallmarks very quickly and take steps to break that spell."To date, the bank that Helen's mum uses has returned £45,000 to her account.Though Helen changed her mum's phone number three times, she continued to give the new one to the scammers. Helen eventually replaced her mum's smartphone with one that could only do calls and texts. Winters also advises "completely resetting" a loved ones digital footprint by changing telephone numbers, email address and social media accounts."That's what makes you visible, that's what puts you out there. So taking steps to reset all of that is so important," he says.

schema.headline: 'Mum sent them £140,000': How to spot the signs a loved one is being scammed

title: Brendan Venter: Saracens face fines after director of rugby refuses media commitments
description: Saracens are set to receive a series of fines from Prem Rugby due to director of rugby Brendan Venter's failure to fulfil media commitments.It is unde
body: Saracens are set to receive a series of fines from Prem Rugby due to director of rugby Brendan Venter's failure to fulfil media commitments.It is understood the club have already been handed a £5,000 sanction after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day.The South African also did not speak to the media before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester.The Daily Telegraph reported earlier on Tuesday, external that Venter "resigned" as director of rugby last month and took up a new role of "head of rugby culture and wine consultant", with head coach Joe Shaw assuming responsibility for media commitments.The report also claims Saracens asked permission in July for Shaw to front the club's media commitments.However, none of this has been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby.It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities.Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning to the club as director of rugby and have yet to confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities.He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 trophy-laden years in the job.Venter's first spell as Sarries' director of rugby, which began in 2009, also included clashes with authorities over media commitments.In September 2010, the club apologised to European Rugby Cup (ERC) officials for then-captain Steve Borthwick's failure to attend the Heineken Cup launch at Cardiff's Millennium Stadium.Borthwick, now England head coach, was the only missing representative from the coaches and captains of 12 English, Welsh and Scottish clubs attending the event.He had been told by Saracens to instead attend a team bonding session at a beer festival in Munich.In December 2010, Venter himself was warned by European Rugby Cup officials for a post-match interview after his side's 24-21 Heineken Cup loss to Racing Metro, in which he repeatedly gave short answers, agreeing with whatever was being asked.He later said it was inspired by a scene in the football mockumentary film, Mike Bassett: England Manager.Venter left his full-time role at Saracens halfway through the 2010–11 season, to be replaced by McCall.

schema.headline: Brendan Venter: Saracens face fines after director of rugby refuses media commitments

title: Blue Lights: The police drama hitting home in Northern Ireland
description: Image source, Peter Marley / BBC / Two Cities TelevisionImage caption, Katherine Devlin's first major role was in Blue Lights as Constable Annie Conlo
body: Image source, Peter Marley / BBC / Two Cities TelevisionImage caption, Katherine Devlin's first major role was in Blue Lights as Constable Annie ConlonByÁine O DonnellBBC Newsbeat"Whether it's your friends or your family, everybody has their own relationships with, and viewpoints on, the police," says Dearbháile McKinney, star of BBC drama Blue Lights.The Londonderry actress and her co-star Katherine Devlin, who also grew up in Northern Ireland, say relationships between police and communities there were at the forefront of their minds as they prepared for filming. The Bafta-winning series follows police officers working at the fictional Blackthorn Station in Belfast.But, for many watching, the drama feels all too real. The difficulty police in Northern Ireland still face was thrown into focus this weekend by the long-running dispute over the controversial Garvaghy Road parade route when officers had to prevent a march by Protestant Orangemen through a largely Catholic area.Many scenes in Blue Lights highlight the distrust of, and hostility towards, the police in some communities. Warning: This article includes spoilers for the first three seasons of Blue Lights. Image source, Peter Marley / BBC / Two Cities TelevisionImage caption, Annie Conlon (Katherine Devlin), Grace Ellis (Siân Brooke) and Tommy Foster (Nathan Braniff) join as new recruits in the first seriesDevlin plays Annie Conlon, whose storyline deals with her having to move away from home as a result of death threats because she's from a Catholic family. "We do have similarities - she comes from a Catholic background and so do I," Devlin tells BBC Newsbeat. "I know girls like Annie."But I've realised we're different in a lot of ways. Mainly, to be honest with you, I wouldn't go into the police." Devlin says that forming Annie's character was about trying to understand why she decided to become an officer and "for that to be the crux of her story". "I think a huge thing with this season is the idea of home and what home means to her," she says."Just battling that inner dialogue that she has with 'is it all worth it?'"Especially her being a Catholic and the intricacies of that and the politics of that. "It's heavy stuff and she has to really think about it."Image source, Peter Marley / BBC / Two Cities TelevisionImage caption, Blue Lights won Best Drama Series at the Baftas in 2025The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) had its lowest number of Catholic applicants in more than a decade earlier this year, with some pointing to "fear and apprehension" in those communities putting them off joining the police. One of the force's aims when it was founded in 2001 was to build broader community support and increase Catholic officers. At the time, only 8% of the force was from that background. It's now at 32%. In a statement sent to Newsbeat, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher said the PSNI was "totally committed to being more representative of the communities we serve". "I am deeply concerned at persistent and often unjustified criticism and the outdated and unsupported views of dissident paramilitaries remaining as barriers to people seeing themselves having a career in the police," he said. Boutcher said he "absolutely" accepted the PSNI needed to do more to diversify its recruitment but could only do so if "people in all communities in Northern Ireland see policing as a career for them".He said the force planned to launch a new student officer recruitment campaign "in the coming weeks".Image source, Peter Marley / BBC / Two Cities TelevisionImage caption, The storyline following the strain on Aisling's relationship with fellow officer Tommy continues in the new seriesBlue Lights is filmed locally and on set in east Belfast you can spot the attention to detail, right down to the information leaflets at a police station reception area and case folders on officers' desks. "It's really lovely just to see the amount of people who see themselves in the characters," Devlin says. "And [mention] how complex the characters are. How real and human they are." It's something McKinney considered in how she plays Aisling Byrne. Aisling struggled with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the last series, something Dearbháile says she spoke to real-life officers about. "They've had to witness some horrific things and been left with PTSD and trauma that they just have to learn to live with," she says."It's the reality here. It would be ignorant to not think about that."Aisling's condition puts a strain on her relationship with Tommy Foster, played by Nathan Braniff, who is then faced with the decision whether to report her to their bosses so she can get help. And while Braniff says Blue Lights often deals with heavy themes, he believes it does a good job at showing what Northern Ireland is really like. "It shows that Northern Ireland's moving forward and changing all the time." Image source, Peter Marley / BBC / Two Cities TelevisionImage caption, Frank Blake had plenty of practice with his Belfast accent after roles in Trespasses and Say NothingOne thing that's changed for the fourth series is the public interest when the actors are filming scenes in Belfast city centre. "After having lived here my whole life, it's funny walking down the streets of Belfast and bumping into people that I know wearing my full police costume," Braniff says."The support for the show here is unmatched."Frank Blake, who plays Shane Bradley, is one of the few actors who isn't from Northern Ireland but he says he felt the same welcome, thanks mainly to a scene where his character opens up about his love of a certain Westlife song."We were shooting in town, and someone drove past blaring World of Our Own out of the speakers," he says."I've long been a Westlife fan and it was great craic. It's so funny seeing how it really took off."Series four of Blue Lights starts at 21:00 BST on BBC One and is available to watch on iPlayer. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Blue Lights: The police drama hitting home in Northern Ireland

title: Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech
description: Image source, EPA ShutterstockByBrian WheelerPolitical reporterAndy Burnham has delivered his first speech to the Labour conference as party leader an
body: Image source, EPA ShutterstockByBrian WheelerPolitical reporterAndy Burnham has delivered his first speech to the Labour conference as party leader and prime minister. Here is what stood out.1. Relaxed vibes, serious contentIt was no surprise to see Andy Burnham tieless and roaming the conference stage in Liverpool, unanchored by the traditional leader's speech podium.But despite the relaxed TED talk vibe, this was sober and serious speech. He set out major new policies - not always a given on these occasions - and spoke with real emotion about his family and working class roots.There were few jokes - and in stark contrast to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's speech last year, he did not mention Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch once. But he also avoided mention of some of the trickier issues he faces, such as welfare reform and how his government will pay for promised increases in defence spending.2. Bringing back public controlMuch of his speech was aimed at the party faithful, with a promise to "break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path", and bring back traditional Labour values.It went down extremely well in the hall. We counted 11 standing ovations in just over an hour.The first came when he vowed to overturn Margaret Thatcher's 1980s reforms to give the public greater control over housing, water and energy.The new part was a plan to legislate later this year to repeal Thatcher's "ideological ban on public ownership of water companies".He said this would put the UK on a 10-year path to a "very different water system" - although there was not an explicit commitment to renationalisation.3. Pensions triple lock gambleThe run up to the speech was dominated by speculation about whether Burnham would scrap the state pension triple lock, which guarantees increases in line with the highest of inflation, earnings or 2.5%.In the end, it was a bit more nuanced than that.He said he would "honour" Labour's commitment to keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament.But from April 2030, the state pension would rise every year by inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, under Burnham's plans - and it will be increased in some years if needed to keep pace with average worker earnings.The change, he said, would "generate significant savings" to fund his long-held ambition of creating a National Care Service in England."I accept I may pay a political price," he told the conference. "But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off."4. Electoral reform cheered by conferenceBurnham has made no secret of his desire to scrap Westminster's first-past-the-post voting system.And his announcement of a national commission on electoral reform went down very well with many in the hall, who have been calling for it."We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard," he said to cheers.5. Emotional tribute to late fatherAs he neared the end of his speech, Burnham appeared overcome by emotion and it looked for a brief moment as though he could not carry on.He was speaking about his father Roy, who he lost to Alzheimer's earlier this month."If only, if only he had been able to appreciate that moment of the family in Downing Street," Burnham said of his first day in his new role."The son of a man who failed his 11-plus becoming prime minister."The longest ovation of all came when he pledged to "use this job to build the kind of Britain my dad wanted to see – and fight with everything I've got to keep it together".Figure caption, Watch: The big announcements in Burnham's conference speechGet in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech

title: Fury vs Joshua: British heavyweights arrive in London for news conference
description: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have both arrived in London before Wednesday's launch news conference for their fight.It appears the all-British heavywe
body: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have both arrived in London before Wednesday's launch news conference for their fight.It appears the all-British heavyweight contest - more than a decade in the making - remains on for 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium following several days of uncertainty.Fury, 38, has travelled back from the United States, where he had been at Walt Disney World Resort with his family, while Joshua, 36, has flown in from his training camp in Dubai.Fury-Joshua was officially announced on Thursday by Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh, but doubts emerged 24 hours later amid a dispute over the role of UFC chief Dana White in the promotion.Broadcaster Netflix said Alalshikh's The Ring and White would collaborate to promote the event, but Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.White said on Saturday night he did not know whether the fight - or Wednesday's news conference - would happen. BBC Sport now understands he will not attend the launch.A further potential hurdle emerged late on Monday over Fury's enrolment in the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (Vada) testing programme.Fury's manager Spencer Brown has since said Fury is now enrolled with Vada, appearing to resolve another issue before the launch.Fury and Joshua have never fought despite several previous attempts to make the all-British contest.Wednesday's event at the British Airways ARC in Olympia will be the first time the pair have come face-to-face since the fight was officially announced, with a limited number of tickets also being made available to the public.There was at least something reassuring about seeing both men step out of cars in London on Tuesday, ready for Wednesday's launch.But a Fury-Joshua fight being 'on' has now been announced so many times it is hard to keep count.And that is part of the problem. We have been here before and there is no way to dress up the past few days as anything other than a desperately poor look for boxing.The majority of supporters felt Fury-Joshua had arrived too late, with both men now former champions and far from the peak of their powers.Yet within 48 hours of the long-awaited announcement, even some of those still excited by the contest had been turned into cynics.Instead of discussing how Fury and Joshua match up, the conversation became about promoters, contractual clauses, competing egos and whether the fight would happen at all.That is remarkable for a shared purse reported to be worth close to $200m (£151m), backed by some of the most powerful figures in the sport.Hearn has alleged contractual terms around White's involvement have not been adhered to. White has publicly attacked Hearn. Fury accused Joshua's camp of trying to pull out.All of it created unnecessary uncertainty around a fight boxing has spent years failing to deliver.With all that said, Wednesday offers an opportunity to change the mood quickly.If Fury and Joshua both walk on stage and produce the kind of fireworks their rivalry had long-promised, some - though not all - of the noise of the past few days could fade.

schema.headline: Fury vs Joshua: British heavyweights arrive in London for news conference

title: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
description: Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.In his first party conference
body: Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system

title: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble
description: It was a significant announcement from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his plans for the triple lock after the general election. It will reverberate we
body: It was a significant announcement from Prime Minister Andy Burnham on his plans for the triple lock after the general election. It will reverberate well beyond the hall.For months, I have heard suggestions that Andy Burnham was warm to the idea that the triple lock as we know it had to go.I had expected him to try to forge a political consensus on this thorny issue at this stage, but he has gone further than that. He has tried to take the sting out of the politics of his decision by tying it to funding a new national social care service.The government calls it an "adjusted triple lock" as it is keen that pensioners are reassured. It is more like a double lock plus. The sensitivity over this political gamble is clear.Under Burnham's plans, the state pension will go up by either the pace of price rises or 2.5%, whichever is higher. So, it will still keep up with inflation and go up every year.The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time. The policy would be to maintain the state pension as a share of earnings at the record level it is due to reach in 2030.This change is sharper than expected. Not a review or a consultation. Ministers and MPs will have to back the plans in interviews and, at some point, MPs will have to vote on changing the historic annual earnings link to the state pension.It seems far more significant than a mere "adjustment". This will save many billions in the coming decades, but not so much in the next few years. The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank says that, had Burnham's tweak been in place since 2011, it would have more than halved the annual £16bn cost of the triple lock, a £9bn saving every year. Government sources said the decision to make the change now will save around £15bn a year by 2040.The prime minister was repeatedly advised that bond markets would show some appreciation for a UK government capable of taking tough decisions. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves might have imagined the same reward for her decision to scrap the winter fuel allowance, which was one of her first acts and later reversed.Part of the UK premium in bond markets has been an understandable perception that UK politics cannot have long-term debates. And the triple lock is only one of the debates started by today's speech – with significant further moves on energy and post-Brexit policy expected – that the prime minister and chancellor need the markets as well as the country to get behind.

schema.headline: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble

title: Three teenagers die after car enters River Wear in Sunderland
description: Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear.Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns
body: Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear.Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and entered the water.Four people were in the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy managed to reach safety. He is currently in hospital with non-serious injuries, and has subsequently been arrested in connection with the incident, the force said.The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water.No other vehicles are believed to have been involved.Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said it was "a truly tragic incident"."Our thoughts are with their families, friends and all those impacted by what has happened," he said.He added the investigation was at an early stage and the force was working to establish the circumstances.

schema.headline: Three teenagers die after car enters River Wear in Sunderland

title: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home
description: Figure caption, Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablazeByYolande KnellMiddle Ea
body: Figure caption, Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablazeByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemMore than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers.Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence."It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC."My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us."Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mahmoud al-Tubasi said he thought settlers were going to kill him and his familyThe family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks.  Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons  who are married with young daughters.Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police.By torchlight, the family inspected one home.  A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about.  The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste.A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped."As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Israel's High Court has ruled that the al-Tubasi family must be allowed to return to their homesThe grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back.  Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle.  As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses.  Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them.Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves."An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces." The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed."The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Israel's prime minister called on law enforcement authorities to prosecute those he called "rioters"One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud.The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago.The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state."Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks.Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence.  He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires."According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction. Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank".Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministers have said they aim to "bury the idea" that an independent Palestinian state could be set up in the territory along with East Jerusalem and Gaza. Settlements and outposts are illegal under international law.Levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, according to the United Nations, which says that since 2023, more than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks and access restrictions in the occupied West Bank.In the same time period, the UN's Humanitarian Office (OCHA) has logged 6,199 attacks by Israeli settlers causing casualties or damage, external.According to OCHA, at least 82 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank this year and four Israelis have been killed - members of the security forces and civilians.  At least 23 Palestinians were killed in the context of settler attacks.

schema.headline: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home

title: I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. Here's why
description: As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful.In July the 21-year-old graduated fro
body: As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful.In July the 21-year-old graduated from Nottingham Trent University with a degree in content creation.As well as teaching how to best make videos and posts for Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, the course also focused on how to build audiences, engage with brands and monetise your content."I always wanted to be an entrepreneur, so for me the course was about the transferable skills that I believed I would gain," says Destiny, pointing to both the social media and business aspects she was taught.It's early on in her career, and Destiny won't disclose precisely what she is earning, but says she's already making money.In addition to posting about fashion on her own accounts, she makes videos for others, and has also been hired as a TikTok live selling host, presenting products for sale on camera.She says the course gave her access to equipment, technology and industry contacts."The incredible people I've met through panels that the university hosted would take someone five to 10 years to get to that place," she explains.Nottingham Trent says its content creation degree, which it launched in 2022, provides "hands-on experience". Several universities in the UK now offer such courses. The University of Brighton says it teaches students how to create "content that cuts through the noise".Meanwhile in the US, Arizona State University say its similar qualification allows students to "turn your creativity into content that connects with audiences". Yet you'd be paying a lot of money for this. The three-year degrees at Nottingham Trent and Brighton both currently cost £9,790 per year for UK students, while the standard annual fee at Arizona State is $14,724 (£11,000) for a resident of that state.So are such degrees worth it? Knightenator, a UK-based, full-time content creator, isn't sure. "I don't think I would have taken the course," she says.The 31-year-old, who doesn't reveal her real name, has been posting videos about gaming and travel on social media since 2015. She now has 65,000 followers on Twitch, and more than 100,000 on TikTok.It is her full-time job, and while she won't reveal how much money she makes, she says she gets most of her income from deals with brands that she promotes."Honestly, from my experience, I don't think companies would care too much if you had a content creator degree," she says.She adds that the internet is saturated with free advice on how to get started. "If you have the drive to want to become a content creator, the tips are out there, and you don't need to commit to a three-year degree."Her advice is to watch other people's content and find your own niche. "I honestly think that you don't need much in this day and age at this moment to be able to do it."But fellow content creator Aiesha Beasley from Phoenix, Arizona disagrees.The 36-year-old, who posts about food, fashion and lifestyle, says she would have enrolled on one of these courses if they had been available when she first started blogging on Tumblr in the early 2010s.She believes a degree would have given her a "clearer pathway", particularly when it comes to how to earn a living."You really do have to have a business mindset on: how can I transition this from a hobby into something that makes me money?" says Aiesha.She adds that such courses are "ahead of the curve" in recognising that content creation is increasingly an important part of marketing."Now you have to have a digital presence," she explains, "whether you are a business owner or an entrepreneur or building a personal brand."The degrees by the likes of Nottingham Trent and Arizona State come as the content creator economy booms on both sides of the Atlantic. YouTube content creators alone contribute £2.2bn to the UK economy, according to one report last year.Meanwhile, one in three people aged between 18 and 30 in the US wish to become an influencer, a 2024 survey suggests. , externalHowever, Jacky Gurr, course leader and senior lecturer for content creation at Nottingham Trent University, points out that the majority of people on the course are not actually aspiring to become influencers.For Gurr, content creation is a professional skill that organisations increasingly need, whether someone runs their own business, works in-house, joins an agency or works freelance across multiple clients."Those skills absolutely can be taught. Students learn how to plan and produce video content, develop campaigns, understand audiences, analyse performance data and adapt strategies based on that data."She adds that the business side of content creation "is an important part of the degree", where they discuss monetisation and the commercial side of the industry.But for anyone who thinks a university degree will lead to overnight success as an influencer, Jacky Gurr has these words of caution: "So much of being a successful influencer is about luck, and we can't teach luck or personality."

schema.headline: I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. Here's why

title: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage in Channel
description: Thomas is alleged to have used his social media platform to livestream himself from the English Channel at around 16:30 BST on 22 September, broadcast
body: Thomas is alleged to have used his social media platform to livestream himself from the English Channel at around 16:30 BST on 22 September, broadcasting to a large audience, the court heard.He is accused of slashing a boat that had been used by migrants, which was adrift in the sea, while a rescue crew member was on board.He is also alleged to have said "this is what needs to happen" and "this is England, this isn't France any more".Simon Pentol KC, defending, had proposed a "package of bail conditions" as an alternative to Thomas being remanded in custody and described the allegation against his client as "politically charged and fundamentally flawed".On his decision to refuse bail, the Judge James Newton-Price KC, said: "I am not concerned with the political issues or motivations in this matter and I put them aside in deciding this matter."A handful of supporters waited outside the court to hear the outcome of the hearing.

schema.headline: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage in Channel
